what_its_for: Pentoxifylline helps improve blood flow in your body. It is used to treat a condition called intermittent claudication, which causes leg pain, cramping, or tiredness when you walk because of poor blood flow. This medicine makes your blood less thick and sticky so it can flow more easily through your blood vessels, helping you walk farther with less pain.
how_to_take: Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablet. Take it with meals or right after eating to help prevent an upset stomach. Try to take it at the same times each day to help you remember.
dosing: The usual adult dose is 400 mg (one tablet) taken three times a day, typically with breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Your doctor may lower your dose to 400 mg twice a day if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store pentoxifylline at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired medicine safely according to your local pharmacy or community guidelines.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking, as it narrows your blood vessels and makes this medicine less effective. Limit or avoid alcohol, as it may increase the risk of side effects like dizziness. Be careful when standing up quickly, as this medicine can sometimes cause dizziness. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines you take, especially blood thinners like warfarin, aspirin, or other pain relievers, as pentoxifylline may increase your risk of bleeding.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience: chest pain or an irregular heartbeat, unusual bleeding or bruising, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, severe dizziness or fainting, a skin rash, itching, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat (signs of an allergic reaction), or severe nausea and vomiting. Also call your doctor if your leg pain does not improve after 8 weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: Pentoxifylline does not work overnight. Most people start to notice some improvement in how far they can walk after about 2 to 4 weeks. The full benefit of the medicine may take up to 8 weeks or longer. Keep taking it as directed even if you do not feel a difference right away, and talk to your doctor if you see no improvement after 8 weeks.
special_populations: Older adults (over 65): You may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness, nausea, or an upset stomach. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Kidney or liver problems: This medicine is processed by your liver and kidneys. If you have kidney or liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The safety of this medicine during pregnancy is not fully known, and it may pass into breast milk. Your doctor will help you decide if the benefits outweigh the risks.
